lesson.title: Voluntary Response: When People Select Themselves
lesson.summary: A voluntary response sample forms when individuals choose on their own whether to participate, typically in response to a broad invitation, which systematically overrepresents people with strong opinions and underrepresents everyone else.
lesson.body:
A voluntary response sample is built from whoever chooses to respond to an open invitation: a call-in poll after a news segment, an online survey link shared on social media, a comment box at a store's exit. Unlike a convenience sample, where the researcher picks who to approach based on what's easy to reach, a voluntary response sample flips the direction of selection entirely, the researcher opens the door to anyone in the population, and it is each individual who decides whether to walk through it. This might sound more inclusive than a convenience sample, but it introduces its own severe and very predictable bias.

The core problem is that the decision to respond is rarely random with respect to the opinion being measured. People with strong feelings, especially strong negative feelings, are far more motivated to spend the time filling out a survey or dialing a call-in number than people with mild or neutral opinions, who often see no reason to bother. A radio station that asks listeners to call in and rate a controversial new policy will hear disproportionately from people who love it and people who hate it, while the much larger group who feel lukewarm or indifferent mostly stays silent, skewing the sample toward the extremes and away from the true center of public opinion.

Consider a hypothetical example. A city posts an online survey asking residents to rate satisfaction with a newly redesigned public park, sharing the link only through the park's own social media page. Over two weeks, 300 people respond. Because the people who follow a park's social media page and take time to fill out an unsolicited survey are disproportionately either enthusiastic regulars who love the redesign or frustrated neighbors upset enough to complain, the 300 responses likely do not reflect the views of the roughly 40,000 residents who live near the park but never saw the post or never felt strongly enough to click through, producing a sample that overstates both the loudest praise and the loudest complaints relative to the broader population's more moderate average opinion.

Voluntary response samples share the same fundamental flaw as convenience samples, both are non-random and therefore both are vulnerable to bias, but the mechanism differs in an instructive way. A convenience sample is biased by the researcher's choice of where to stand; a voluntary response sample is biased by the respondent's choice of whether to speak up, and that self-selection tends specifically to amplify strong or extreme opinions relative to their true prevalence in the population. This makes voluntary response samples especially treacherous for any question involving controversy, satisfaction, or complaint, exactly the topics most likely to motivate a lopsided response.

Increasing the number of voluntary responses does not fix the underlying problem, a call-in poll with 50,000 votes is not more trustworthy than one with 500 votes if both draw from the same self-selected, opinion-skewed pool; the sample simply becomes a larger version of the same biased slice of the population. As with convenience samples, the standard statistical machinery for estimating a margin of error assumes the sample came from a random process, an assumption voluntary response sampling violates by its very design, so any percentage reported from a voluntary response poll should be treated as a description of who chose to respond, not a reliable estimate of the broader population's views.
